t.2.31.1: Sent by Rāma, the charioteer, his senses clouded with anguish, quickly entered and saw the king sighing heavily.
t.2.31.2: Seeing him utterly distraught in mind and grieving for Rāma alone, the very wise charioteer approached with joined palms.
t.2.31.4: May Rāma, whose valour is truth, see you, blessings upon you. Having taken leave of all his friends, he now wishes to see you.
t.2.31.5: He will go to the great forest. Behold him, O lord of the earth, endowed with all royal virtues, like the sun surrounded by its rays.
t.2.31.3: Here at your door, O tiger among men, stands your son, having given away all his wealth to the brāhmaṇas and to those who depend on him.
t.2.31.6: That king, truthful in speech and righteous in spirit, like the ocean in his depth and spotless as the sky, replied to him.
t.2.31.7: Sumantra, bring my wives, all those who are mine here. Surrounded by all my wives, I wish to see Rāghava.
t.2.31.8: Having passed into the inner apartments, he spoke these words to those women: "The noble king summons you; go there without delay."
t.2.31.9: Thus addressed by Sumantra at the king's command, all the women, having understood their lord's order, proceeded to that palace.
t.2.31.10: Then those three hundred and fifty women, their eyes red with weeping and steadfast in their vows, surrounded Kausalyā and slowly went forth.
t.2.31.11: When his wives had arrived, the lord of the earth looked upon them, and the king said to the charioteer, "Sumantra, bring my son to me."
t.2.31.12: Then that charioteer, taking Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa and Maithilī with him, went swiftly straight toward the presence of the lord of the earth.
t.2.31.13: Seeing from afar his son approaching with joined palms, the anguished king, surrounded by his women, sprang up swiftly from his seat.
t.2.31.14: Seeing Rāma, the lord of the people rushed toward him with great speed; but before he could reach him, stricken with grief, he fell fainting to the ground.
t.2.31.15: Then Rāma swiftly rushed toward him, and so did Lakṣmaṇa, the great chariot-warrior, toward the grief-stricken king, who seemed to have lost his senses through sorrow.
t.2.31.16: And suddenly in the king's palace there arose the wailing of a thousand women, crying "Alas, alas, Rāma!", swelled by the jingling of their ornaments.
t.2.31.18: Then, after a moment, Rāma, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to the lord of the earth, who had regained consciousness but was drowned in an ocean of grief.
t.2.31.17: Embracing him with their arms, both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, together with Sītā, weeping, laid him down upon the couch.
t.2.31.19: I take my leave of you, great king, for you are the lord of us all. Look upon me with good wishes as I set out for the Daṇḍaka forest.
t.2.31.20: Grant leave to Lakṣmaṇa as well, for Sītā too follows me to the forest; though held back with many sound reasons, the two of them do not wish to stay.
t.2.31.21: Casting off your grief, O giver of honour, grant leave to all of us, to Lakṣmaṇa, to me, and to Sītā, as Prajāpati grants leave to his creatures.
t.2.31.22: Seeing Rāghava, who was calmly awaiting the permission of the lord of the earth for his dwelling in the forest, the king spoke to him.
t.2.31.23: O Rāghava, I have been deluded by the granting of a boon to Kaikeyī; restrain me and become king of Ayodhyā yourself this very day.
t.2.31.24: Thus addressed by the king, Rāma, foremost among the upholders of dharma and skilled in speech, folded his hands in reverence and replied to his father.
t.2.31.25: O king, may you be lord of the earth for a thousand years, while I shall dwell in the forest; no falsehood should be committed by you for my sake.
t.2.31.26: For your welfare, for your prosperity, and for your return again, dear son, go calmly along an auspicious road that holds no danger from any quarter.
t.2.31.27: But now, today, my son, do not go at all this night; spend this night here, looking upon your mother and me. Gratified with every object of desire, you shall set out at the break of tomorrow.
t.2.31.28: Then Rāma, having heard thus the words of his anguished father, spoke these words in sorrow, together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa.
t.2.31.29: The merits I shall gain today, who will bestow them on me tomorrow? Therefore, with all my desires, I choose departure alone.
t.2.31.30: Let this earth, with its kingdoms and its peoples, teeming with wealth and grain, which I have relinquished, be given to Bharata.
t.2.31.31: Let your sorrow depart; do not be overwhelmed with tears. For the ocean, lord of rivers, invincible, is never agitated.
t.2.31.32: I do not desire the kingdom, nor happiness, nor even Maithilī; what I desire, O bull among men, is that you be truthful, not false.
t.2.31.33: Let the city, the kingdom and the entire earth, all relinquished by me, be given to Bharata. Obeying your command, I shall go to the forest to dwell there for a long time.
t.2.31.34: Let Bharata alone rule this earth, relinquished by me, with its mountain ranges, its cities and its forests, auspicious and well-bounded; O king, let what you have spoken be fulfilled.
t.2.31.35: O king, my mind is not so set upon great pleasures, nor upon what is dear to myself, as it is upon your command, which the virtuous approve. Let your sorrow on my account depart, O sinless one.
t.2.31.37: Having entered the forest with its wondrous trees, eating fruits and roots there and gazing upon mountains, rivers and lakes, I shall be happy. Let your mind be at ease.
t.2.31.36: Therefore today, O sinless one, I would not choose imperishable kingship, nor all my desires, nor happiness, nor Maithilī, nor even life itself, if it meant binding you to a falsehood; let your vow stand true, just as it was given.
